strengths: The paper addresses a relevant NLP problem: forecasting pre-training loss to support hyperparameter selection directly on the target model. The token-position decomposition offers an interpretable perspective on learning dynamics.

The experiments cover 468M and 1.2B models trained for 400B tokens, with both Pile and C4 validation. The reported position-wise fits are strong, and forecasting from early training portions provides evidence beyond fitting complete trajectories.

The data-mixture application reports lower perplexity in all four model/dataset settings and improvements in 12 of 14 downstream model/benchmark comparisons. These results provide an encouraging practical demonstration.
The appendices document model configurations, several training hyperparameters, software versions, and position-weighting interventions, providing useful reproducibility information.
weaknesses: The central power-law comparison requires correction or explanation. Table 1 reports approximately −2.4 to −2.9 R² when fitting complete trajectories with (p1*x)^p2+p3. This family contains the constant mean predictor through p2=0 and an appropriate p3, so its global least-squares optimum cannot have negative in-sample R². These results suggest optimization failure, an evaluation error, or undocumented constraints; they do not establish that power laws cannot describe the trajectories. This directly undermines a central comparative claim.

The contribution of token-position decomposition is not isolated. After a0 and a1 are frozen, Eqs. (8), (10), and (14) make aggregate loss a constant plus a cosine using the known training schedule. The baselines receive neither this schedule dependence nor comparable piecewise flexibility. An aggregate-loss baseline using the same temporal functional family is necessary to establish why position-wise modeling improves prediction.

The breadth of the claims exceeds the validation. Both target models use one training corpus, a 1024-token context, and the same 400B-token cosine schedule. The functional forms are motivated by inspecting complete trajectories, without a clearly independent set of runs for evaluating those modeling choices. Generalization across schedules and training horizons remains untested. The claim that temporal scaling was previously unexplored also needs qualification against Kaplan et al.'s training-step analysis.

The hyperparameter-selection evidence is incomplete. Selection uses 10B tokens, only 2.5% of training, whereas Figure 3 validates forecasting from 10–40%. Predicted versus actual losses and ranking accuracy across the five candidates are not reported. The perplexity improvements are modest, and no independent-run uncertainty is provided; averaging the last five checkpoints does not establish robustness across training runs.

The interpretation of position weighting is stronger than the evidence supports. Equation (17) follows from manually freezing a0 and a1, rather than independently establishing optimal training weights. Figure 6 supports approximately uniform observed loss reductions, but those reductions do not imply that alternative weighting objectives cannot help. Three fixed suppression strategies applied after the separation point support only a limited conclusion that uniform weighting remains competitive in these experiments.

Important implementation details remain unspecified: nonlinear-fitting initialization and bounds, convergence checks, the residual-outlier filtering threshold, checkpoint sampling frequency, actual candidate mixture vectors, and the search budget. No fitting implementation or loss traces are linked. These omissions are particularly consequential given the anomalous baseline fits and prevent confident reproduction of the central results.
